implementation_notes: Go has no classes, so the canonical C++ poltergeist cannot be written in idiomatic Go — but the equivalent appears constantly as a struct with one field and no methods, constructed and immediately used. Go's own idiom is a package-level function, so the deletion is also a simplification rather than a refactoring. The support level is discouraged because a struct that exists only to be constructed, used once and discarded has no representation in Go's idiom: `go vet` will not complain, but a linter for single-field structs with no methods will, and any function taking `*T` for such a type is an indirection with no purpose.
idiom_name: single-use struct; Go has no reason for one
alternative: Delete the struct and call the package-level function that owns the behaviour; if the operation genuinely needs state, define a named type with value semantics and methods on it.
pitfalls: A struct used as a named result/option bundle (`type options struct{...}`) is a legitimate parameter object, not a poltergeist.
Interfaces satisfied by the single-use struct are the rescue that makes it live; check for an interface implementation before deleting.
Constructors returning a pointer to a single-field struct are a common pattern for immutability and are fine when the type has more than one field.
